steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half like a card. This is your jungle page.
On the folded edge, cut two short parallel slits about 4 cm apart. Do not cut all the way across.
Open the card and push the strip between the slits inwards so it pops forward. That is your first jungle platform.
Draw and cut out a tall tree, then glue it to the front of the popped-out strip.
Draw an animal that lives in a jungle. Colour it so it almost matches the tree behind it.
Glue the animal on and close the book. Open it for someone and see how long they take to spot the animal.
activities.title: The Pop-Up Jungle Book
activities.summary: Build a jungle that stands up off the page, then hide an animal so well that a grown-up needs three guesses.

learning.text: Some animals have colours and patterns that match where they live. It makes them hard to spot, which helps them stay safe or sneak up on food. Your paper animal just did the same trick.
learning.title: Camouflage helps animals hide in plain sight

activities.variation: Add a second pop-up layer behind the first so the jungle has depth. Try a river, a cave, or a night-time version with a paper moon.
safetyNotes: A grown-up should be nearby for the cutting steps.
Cut away from your body, and keep the closed scissors pointing down when you walk.
materialsDetail: 3 sheets of paper or thin card
activities.discussionPrompt: If your animal moved to a snowy place instead of a jungle, what colour would it need to be?

steps: Choose a start and a finish. Lay the route between them with tape, string, or track.
Walk the route slowly and look for three places that feel risky: a sharp turn, a narrow bridge, a crossing.
Make one sign for each risky spot. Draw the picture first, then add the word.
Build a signal station at the busiest point. It needs somewhere for a signaller to stand and something that changes: a flag, a flipping card, a paper arrow.
Run the train through once with all the signals set to stop. Then run it again with them set to go.
Give someone else the signal job and watch them run the route.
activities.title: The Toy Train Signal Station
activities.summary: Lay a route through the house or the yard, then invent the signs that keep every passenger safe.

learning.text: A signal gives a driver time to slow down, wait, or turn. That is why they sit before the risky part of a journey rather than at it. Every crossing you have ever walked over works this way.
learning.title: Signs and signals tell people what to do before they need to do it

activities.variation: Add a timetable. Give the train a departure time and see whether the signals can keep it running on schedule.
safetyNotes: Keep the route off stairs and away from doorways people walk through.
materialsDetail: Toy train, cars, or anything with wheels
Books or blocks to build a bridge
activities.discussionPrompt: Which of your signs would still make sense to someone who could not read the words?

steps: Bury the dinosaurs while nobody is watching. Remember roughly where they went.
Build a fossil finder from cardboard: a handle, a scoop, and a window to look through.
Mark the dig site into four squares with sticks or string. Diggers work one square at a time.
Brush, do not dig. Sweep the surface away slowly with the spoon or brush.
When you find something, do not pull it out. Draw where it was lying first.
Line up every find in the order you discovered it and tell the story of the site.
activities.title: The Dinosaur Toy Trail
activities.summary: Turn a patch of dirt or a tray of sand into a dig site, and build the tool that finds what is buried.

learning.text: Fossils are not the animal itself. They are the shape it left in rock, or the hard parts that turned to stone over a very long time. That is why the position a fossil is found in tells scientists so much.
learning.title: A fossil is a trace left behind by something that lived long ago

activities.variation: Swap roles. One person buries a set of objects and writes clues, the other one digs using only the clues.
safetyNotes: Wash hands after digging.
A grown-up should check the dig patch for sharp objects first.
materialsDetail: Dinosaur toys or any small figures
A patch of dirt, sand, or a tray of rice
Cardboard and tape for a finder tool
activities.discussionPrompt: What is one question you would ask your dinosaur if it could answer?

steps: Sit down outside and close your eyes for a slow count of sixty.
Open your eyes and write down every sound you can still remember hearing.
Go back and listen again, this time for sounds you missed. Add them to the list.
Next to each sound, write whether it was long or short, high or low, once or over and over.
Make each sound yourself using your voice, your hands, or something from the kitchen.
Put four of them in an order that repeats, and you have a song. Perform it for somebody.
activities.title: The Backyard Sound Song
activities.summary: Sit still outside for four minutes, collect every sound you hear, then turn the list into a song.

learning.text: Birds call to warn each other, to claim a spot, and to find a partner. The call is short and repeated so it carries a long way and is easy to recognise. Your ears just did the same job a listening bird does.
learning.title: Animals use sound to send messages

activities.variation: Record the same spot at a different time of day. Which sounds vanished and which new ones arrived?
safetyNotes: Stay within sight of a grown-up.
If you are near a road, sit facing away from it and stay behind a fence or gate.
materialsDetail: Optional: cups, a box, a comb, anything that makes a noise
activities.discussionPrompt: Which sound was hardest to notice, and why do you think you missed it the first time?

steps: Collect five things that make five different sounds. Tap each one and listen.
Put them in order from lowest sound to highest sound.
Clap a pattern of four: loud, quiet, quiet, loud. Say it out loud until your hands can do it without you thinking.
Play that same pattern on your lowest drum.
Add a second pattern on a higher drum that fits in the gaps.
Teach the pattern to someone else and play it together twice through.
activities.title: The Rainy-Day Drumbeat
activities.summary: A cancelled afternoon turns into a kitchen drum kit and a beat the whole house can clap along to.

learning.text: A beat only becomes a rhythm when it comes back around. Once your ears learn the pattern, they start predicting it, which is why a good rhythm makes people want to move before they decide to.
learning.title: Rhythm is a pattern of sound that repeats

activities.variation: Make it a call and response. One person plays two beats, the other answers with two different ones.
safetyNotes: Nothing made of glass.
Agree on a stop signal before you start, so the drumming can end without an argument.
materialsDetail: A tea towel to soften anything too loud
activities.discussionPrompt: What is a rhythm you hear every day without thinking about it?

steps: Colour or wash the whole page blue first, and let it dry. Reefs live underwater, so the water goes down before anything else.
Draw the reef floor as a bumpy line across the bottom third of the page.
Build the reef upward with three shapes: branches, domes, and fans. Overlap them so gaps appear between them.
Fill in colour, but leave the gaps dark. Those gaps are the important part.
Now add sea creatures. Every creature has to be near a gap it could hide in.
Add one creature that is very hard to find, and challenge someone to find it.
activities.title: The Coral Reef Drawing
activities.summary: Draw a reef packed so full of hiding places that every fish you add has somewhere to go.

learning.text: A reef is built by tiny living animals called coral polyps. All those branches and gaps make hiding places and feeding grounds, which is why a small patch of reef can hold more kinds of creature than the open water around it.
learning.title: Coral reefs give sea animals food and shelter

activities.variation: Draw the same reef at night. Which creatures come out and which ones tuck away?
safetyNotes: Cover the table if you are using anything wet.
materialsDetail: Optional: blue paint or a blue wash for the water
activities.discussionPrompt: What would happen to the creatures in your drawing if the reef disappeared?

steps: Draw the edge of your garden first. A wall, a hedge, a fence, or a river.
Add three paths that go somewhere interesting and one path that goes nowhere.
Draw flowers along the paths. Give at least four of them a shape nobody has seen before.
Add a key in the corner: a small symbol for flowers, insects, water, and hidden things.
Build a viewer from the cardboard tube so you can look at one small patch of map at a time.
Take the viewer outside and find three real things that could belong on your map.
activities.title: The Secret Garden Map
activities.summary: Map a garden that does not exist yet, then build a viewer and go looking for the parts that do.

learning.text: When a bee lands to feed, pollen sticks to its body. It carries that pollen to the next flower without meaning to, and that is how many plants make seeds. A small visitor doing a small job keeps a whole garden growing.
learning.title: Bees move pollen from flower to flower

activities.variation: Draw the map again from above, like a bird would see it, then compare the two versions.
safetyNotes: If you go looking outdoors, stay where a grown-up can see you.
Look at insects. Do not pick them up.
materialsDetail: A cardboard tube or a strip of card
Optional: clear plastic from packaging for a lens
activities.discussionPrompt: Who else in your garden does a small job that matters?

steps: Mark out your stage with tape or a rug. Everything outside the line is backstage.
Pick your song and count the beat out loud: one, two, three, four. Keep counting until it feels automatic.
Invent four moves. Give each one a name so you can remember the order.
Put the moves in a sequence and repeat it twice through, counting the whole way.
Decide what the dance is about. Not the words, the feeling. Then adjust one move to show it more clearly.
Make tickets, hang the curtain, and perform it for one person.
activities.title: The Ballet Story Stage
activities.summary: Build a stage out of a doorway, then choreograph a story that has no words in it at all.

learning.text: Counting turns music into a shared map. When everyone counts the same beats, everyone arrives at the same move at the same moment, even without looking at each other.
learning.title: Dancers count beats to stay together

activities.variation: Teach the sequence to somebody who has never done it. Notice which move is hardest to explain.
safetyNotes: Clear the floor of anything you could trip on before you dance.
Bare feet or grippy socks, not slippery ones.
materialsDetail: A sheet or blanket for a curtain
activities.discussionPrompt: You practised the same four moves several times. What got easier between the first try and the last?

steps: Stand in a line, everybody facing the same way.
Learn the first three steps: right, together, right. Say it out loud as you do it.
Add three more: left, together, left. Now you have six.
Add a quarter turn at the end so the line faces a new wall each time through.
Run the whole sequence four times, once for each wall, until you finish where you started.
Bring in somebody who has never done it and teach them the first three steps only.
activities.title: The Country Line-Dance Barn
activities.summary: Learn a six-step sequence, then teach it to a beginner and find out how patient you can be.

learning.text: Change the order and it becomes a different dance. That is what makes a sequence teachable: once you name the steps and fix the order, anybody can learn it, and everybody ends up in the same place.
learning.title: A sequence is a set of steps in a fixed order

activities.variation: Invent a new ending step as a group, and add it once everyone has the first six.
safetyNotes: Give every dancer an arm's length of space in every direction.
materialsDetail: One song with a strong steady beat
activities.discussionPrompt: When you were teaching, what did you do to help when your learner got stuck?

steps: Read one page about the ocean and pick a single fact that surprised you.
Cut a round porthole in the side of the box and tape clear plastic behind it.
Build a control panel on the inside: dials from bottle caps, switches from folded card, one big lever.
Label one control after the fact you found. If your fact was about depth, build a depth gauge.
Draw what is outside the porthole on a strip of paper, and slide it past the window like a film.
Take somebody on a dive. Narrate what they see and work your fact into the journey.
activities.title: The Library Book Portal Submarine
activities.summary: Read one page about the ocean, then build the submarine that takes you down into it.

learning.text: Two hearts push blood to the gills, where it picks up oxygen, and the third pushes it round the rest of the body. When an octopus swims, the third heart stops, which is one reason octopuses would usually rather crawl.
learning.title: An octopus has three hearts

activities.variation: Swap the ocean for space, a cave, or the inside of a volcano. The submarine becomes a different vehicle entirely.
safetyNotes: A grown-up cuts the porthole hole.
Keep small parts away from anyone under three.
materialsDetail: Bottle caps, buttons, and lids for dials
Clear packaging plastic for a porthole
activities.discussionPrompt: Which fact from the book made you want to look something else up?

steps: Decide what has gone missing. Make it small and oddly specific: a golden leaf, a left shoe, a key that opens nothing.
Write down three characters. One of them knows something they have not said.
Plant three clues. Two should point somewhere useful and one should point the wrong way on purpose.
Build a clue-finder from card: a frame, a handle, and a window you look through.
Write the ending last. The solution has to use at least two of your clues.
Read it aloud to someone and stop before the ending. Let them guess first.
activities.title: The Mystery in the Storybook
activities.summary: Write a mystery about something missing, then build the tool your detective needs to solve it.

learning.text: A leaf is a solar panel with a job. It takes sunlight, water, and air, and makes the sugar the tree needs to grow. That is why leaves are wide and flat, and why a tree in shade grows slowly.
learning.title: Leaves catch sunlight and turn it into food

activities.variation: Give the same three clues to a friend and let them write a completely different ending.
safetyNotes: If you use a real magnifying glass, never point it at the sun.
activities.discussionPrompt: Your false clue sent the reader the wrong way. Why does a mystery need one?

steps: Draw a circle on your plate and divide it into six wedges. Colour each wedge a different colour with markers.
Go outside and hunt for something that matches each wedge. Fallen leaves, petals, stones, bark, seed heads.
Stick each find into the wedge that matches it best.
Look at the two wedges you found hardest to fill. What colours were they?
Mix two of your marker colours together on scrap paper and see if you can make a colour you were missing.
Hang the wheel up somewhere and add to it over the week as the seasons change what is on the ground.
activities.title: The Nature Colour Wheel
activities.summary: Collect colour from outside instead of a paint box, and arrange it into a wheel.

learning.text: Those three are the starting points. Mix any two and you get orange, green, or purple. That is why a colour wheel puts them opposite what they make, and why so few paints can produce so many colours.
learning.title: Red, yellow, and blue mix into every other colour

activities.variation: Do it again in a different season, or in a different place, and hang the two wheels side by side.
safetyNotes: Pick up things that have already fallen. Leave growing plants where they are.
A grown-up should check anything you find before you touch it, and nothing goes in mouths.
materialsDetail: A paper plate or circle of card
Double-sided tape or a glue stick
activities.discussionPrompt: Which colour was hardest to find outside, and why do you think nature has less of it?

steps: Cut out three cube nets, or fold three small paper boxes.
On cube one, draw six characters. On cube two, six places. On cube three, six problems.
Fold and tape all three into cubes.
Roll all three. You now have a character, a place, and a problem you did not choose.
Tell the story out loud in under a minute. No stopping to think, no starting over.
Roll again and hand the cubes to somebody else.
activities.title: The Story Cube Storm
activities.summary: Make three cubes, roll them, and tell the story you are given rather than the one you planned.

learning.text: The beginning tells us who and where. The middle is where the problem shows up. The end is where something changes. Once you know those three parts, you can build a story out of almost any three things.
learning.title: A story needs a beginning, a middle, and an end

activities.variation: Add a fourth cube with six objects on it, and make the object solve the problem.
safetyNotes: A grown-up can help with the cube folds if the card is stiff.
activities.discussionPrompt: Which roll gave you the hardest combination, and how did you make it work anyway?

steps: Ask everybody in the house for one word about your family.
Turn each word into a simple shape or symbol.
Choose three colours and give each one a meaning.
Arrange the symbols on the flag. Big things go in the middle.
Write the key on the back so anybody can read the flag.
activities.title: The Family Flag
activities.summary: Design a flag that says something true about the people you live with.

learning.text: A shape on a flag can stand for an idea, a place, or a promise. Once people agree what a symbol means, it works faster than a sentence.
learning.title: Symbols carry meaning without words

activities.variation: Design a second flag for a made-up country and compare what you chose to put on each.
safetyNotes: Nothing sharp needed for this one.
activities.discussionPrompt: Whose word was hardest to turn into a shape, and how did you solve it?

image.alt: Chike standing in his treehouse workshop holding a drawing tablet and an oversized pencil

steps: Measure something you know well: your bed, a doorway, the kitchen table. Write the numbers down.
Decide how big one square on your paper is going to be. One square equals half a metre works well.
Draw the floor of your treehouse to that scale. Use your bed measurement to check it is big enough to lie down in.
Add the walls and label where the door and windows go.
Draw a second picture from the side, showing how high it sits and how you get up.
Write a materials list at the bottom, with how much of each thing you would need.
activities.title: Draw the Treehouse You Would Build
activities.summary: Plan a treehouse properly, on paper, with measurements you actually worked out.

learning.text: When every measurement shrinks by the same amount, the drawing stays true. That is how a builder can hold a whole house on one page and still know exactly where the door goes.
learning.title: A scale drawing shrinks something big without changing its shape

activities.variation: Draw the same treehouse for somebody with different needs: a ramp instead of a ladder, a wider door, a lower window.
safetyNotes: Measuring a real tree stays on the ground. Nobody climbs to check anything.
materialsDetail: A tape measure if you have one
activities.discussionPrompt: Which measurement surprised you the most when you wrote it down?

steps: Tape one ramp near the top of your wall, tilted gently downward.
Drop the marble. Note exactly where it leaves the ramp and lands.
Tape the next ramp so it starts where the marble landed, tilted the other way.
Keep going down the wall, alternating direction. Add walls of folded card wherever the marble flies off.
Make one ramp steeper than the rest and watch what it does to the speed.
Put a cup at the bottom and run it five times. Count how many times it lands in the cup.
activities.title: The Bottle-Cap Marble Run
activities.summary: Tape a run down a wall and get the marble to the bottom without it ever leaving the track.

learning.text: Gravity pulls straight down all the time. A steep ramp lets more of that pull go into speeding the marble along, so it picks up speed faster. A gentle ramp turns the same drop into a longer, slower journey.
learning.title: A steeper ramp gives a faster roll

activities.variation: Add a jump: a gap the marble has to fly across into a funnel. Adjust the ramp before it until it works.
safetyNotes: Masking tape only, so the wall survives.
Marbles are a choking hazard. Keep them away from anyone under three, and collect them all at the end.
materialsDetail: A marble or a large dried bean
A wall, door, or big box to build on
activities.discussionPrompt: Where did your marble keep escaping, and what finally kept it on the track?

steps: Stretch the four rubber bands around the box, across the hole, spaced apart.
Slide a pencil underneath the bands at each end so they lift off the box.
Pluck each band and listen. Put them in order from lowest to highest.
Look at the ones that sounded highest. What do they have in common?
Now move one pencil closer to the other and pluck the same band again.
Work out how to play three different notes on a single band, then play a tune.
activities.title: The Rubber-Band Guitar
activities.summary: Stretch four bands over a box and work out why some of them sing higher than others.

learning.text: A plucked band vibrates back and forth. Thin, tight, short bands vibrate faster, and faster vibrations reach your ear as a higher note. Every stringed instrument is built around this one idea.
learning.title: Tighter and thinner strings make higher sounds

activities.variation: Fill the box halfway with rice and play it again. What changed?
safetyNotes: Rubber bands snap. Point the box away from faces while you stretch them on.
A grown-up cuts the hole in the box.
materialsDetail: An empty tissue box or a shoebox with a hole cut in the lid
activities.discussionPrompt: How is your box like a real guitar, and what is the box itself doing to the sound?

steps: Cut a rectangle of cardboard for the car body.
Tape two straws underneath as axle housings, then thread the skewers through and fix a wheel on each end. Check they spin freely.
Tape a mast upright in the middle of the body.
Cut a square sail, tape it to the mast, and test it. Mark where the car stopped.
Swap the square for a triangle of the same size and test again from the same start line. Mark it.
Try a third shape of your own. Measure all three distances and decide which sail won.
activities.title: The Wind-Powered Sail Car
activities.summary: Build a car with no engine, then find out what shape of sail carries it furthest.

learning.text: Moving air is made of countless tiny particles bumping into whatever is in the way. A sail gives them a big surface to push against, and that push travels through the mast into the car.
learning.title: Wind pushes a sail, and the sail pushes the car

activities.variation: Keep the winning sail and change the wheels instead. Wide wheels, narrow wheels, four wheels, three.
safetyNotes: A grown-up handles the skewers and caps the ends.
Test in an open space away from roads.
materialsDetail: 4 bottle caps or card circles for wheels
A hand fan or a breezy day
activities.discussionPrompt: Your three sails were the same size but travelled different distances. What else, apart from size, seems to matter?

image.alt: An adult and a child building together with coloured wooden blocks at a table

steps: Write six feelings on six slips of paper and fold them up.
One person picks a slip without showing anybody.
They have five seconds to freeze into a shape that shows that feeling. Whole body, no face-pulling and no words.
Everyone else guesses. The guesser has to say which part of the shape gave it away.
Swap and repeat until every slip has been used.
Pick the two hardest ones and try them again as a pair, working together.
activities.title: Freeze-Frame Feelings
activities.summary: Show a feeling with your whole body and no words, then see if anybody can read it.

learning.text: Shoulders, hands, and posture tell people how you feel from right across a room. Actors and dancers use this on purpose, and everybody else does it without noticing.
learning.title: Bodies communicate before words do

activities.variation: Make it a chain: each new freeze has to connect to the one before it, building a whole scene.
safetyNotes: Freeze on the spot. No running to get into position.
activities.discussionPrompt: Which feeling was hardest to show without your face, and what did you use instead?

image.alt: Zech and Chike hold up a folded paper creature and a paper dinosaur inside the treehouse

steps: Fold one sheet in half the long way, then open it back up. That crease is your centre line.
Fold the two top corners down to the centre crease so they meet in a point.
Fold the whole pointed top down again to the centre, then fold the plane in half along the first crease.
Fold each wing down so it lines up with the bottom edge. Press every crease firmly.
Throw it once. Watch where it goes: high, low, left, or right.
On the second sheet, draw the flight as a map. Mark the launch spot, the curve of the flight, and the landing zone.
activities.title: The Paper Airplane Sky Map
activities.summary: Fold a plane, then draw the map of where it flew. Two brothers, one sheet of paper, and a whole sky to chart.

learning.text: You cannot see air, but a paper airplane can. Air pushes back against the wings, and that push is what holds the plane up. When the plane dips or curves, it is showing you what the air is doing.
learning.title: Wind is moving air

activities.variation: Add a paperclip to the nose and fly it again. Draw a second flight path on the same map in a different colour, then compare the two.
safetyNotes: Fly the plane away from faces, pets, and windows.
Paper edges can give a papercut - press folds with a flat finger, not a fingernail.
materialsDetail: A ruler if you want crisp folds
activities.discussionPrompt: Your first throw did not go where you expected. What is one thing you would change about the plane before the next throw?

steps: Stand the cup in the middle of the tray. This is the crater.
Press clay around the cup to build the mountain. Leave the top of the cup open.
Carve ridges and rivers down the sides with a blunt pencil. Real volcanoes are not smooth.
Build a simple camera rig from cardboard: a base, two upright sides, and a shelf to rest a phone or tablet on so it points at the crater.
Put two spoons of baking soda and a squeeze of dish soap into the crater.
Start recording, then a grown-up pours in the vinegar. Watch the flow instead of the screen.
activities.title: The Clay Volcano Camera Rig
activities.summary: Mateo sculpts the mountain, Chike builds the camera rig, and the two ideas turn into one eruption you can film.

learning.text: Deep under the ground, rock gets so hot that it turns into a thick liquid called magma. When it finds a way out through a volcano, we call it lava. It cools down and hardens into new rock.
learning.title: Lava is melted rock from beneath the surface

activities.variation: Film it a second time from ground level, like a tiny person standing at the foot of the mountain. Compare the two shots.
safetyNotes: A grown-up runs the eruption step and handles the vinegar.
Do this on a tray, outside or over a sink. It will spill on purpose.
Nobody tastes anything, even though it looks like a kitchen experiment.
materialsDetail: A small cup or bottle for the crater
Cardboard and tape for the camera rig
Baking soda, vinegar, and a drop of dish soap
activities.discussionPrompt: Mateo made the volcano and Chike made the camera rig. What did each idea add that the other one could not?

image.alt: Four children building and decorating a house out of cardboard on a playroom floor

steps: Sort the boxes into tall ones and flat ones. Tall boxes become buildings, flat ones become roads and bridges.
Lay out the roads first, then place the buildings along them. A city needs somewhere to go, not just somewhere to be.
Cut a strip of card and lay it flat across a gap to make your first bridge. Push down gently in the middle and watch it sag.
Now fold the same strip into a zigzag so it makes triangles from the side, and lay it across again. Push down again.
Rebuild your weakest bridge using the triangle trick.
Build a small rescue vehicle that has to cross every bridge in the city without any of them collapsing.
activities.title: The Cardboard City Rescue
activities.summary: Build a city out of boxes, then find out which bridges survive when the storm rolls in.

learning.text: Push on a square and it squashes into a slant. Push on a triangle and it stays a triangle, because none of its corners can move without one of its sides changing length. That is why bridges and roofs are full of them.
learning.title: Triangles hold their shape under pressure

activities.variation: Give the city a river made of blue paper and see how many different bridge shapes can cross it.
safetyNotes: A grown-up cuts any thick cardboard.
Build low first. A tall tower that falls is not a disaster, but it should not fall on anybody.
materialsDetail: A pile of boxes, big and small
Anything recyclable that looks like a building
activities.discussionPrompt: Which bridge did you fix first, and how did you decide which one was the weakest?

steps: Empty the clean recycling onto a towel and sort it into big, medium, and small.
Pick your biggest piece for the body and stand it up. Everything else attaches to this.
Add a head, then arms, then legs. Test after each part that the robot still stands.
Give it a face using bottle caps and lids. The eyes decide the whole personality, so try three sets before you commit.
Add one detail that tells you what your robot is for: a scoop, an antenna, a pocket.
Name it and write a three-sentence introduction: what it is called, what it does, and what it is afraid of.
activities.title: The Recycled Robot Friend
activities.summary: Give the recycling bin a second job and end up with a robot that has a name and a personality.

learning.text: Every tin and tub in your robot was on its way to becoming something else. Reusing something as it is takes even less energy than melting it down, which is why building with it counts too.
learning.title: Recycling means a material gets used again instead of thrown away

activities.variation: Build a second robot from only the pieces the first one rejected, and introduce them to each other.
safetyNotes: Only use clean containers, and nothing with a sharp cut edge.
A grown-up checks every tin before it goes in the pile.
materialsDetail: Clean tins, tubs, boxes, and lids
Foil, string, and bottle caps for details
activities.discussionPrompt: Which piece of rubbish turned out to be the most useful, and what made it good?

image.alt: Chike smiling beside screens showing planets and orbit diagrams inside the treehouse

steps: Cut a circle of thick cardboard for the base and mark the sun in the centre.
Draw four rings around the sun, each one further out than the last.
Roll four planets from clay: two small and rocky for the inner rings, two larger for the outer ones.
Push a taped skewer through each planet and anchor it to the base so it can swing around the sun.
Spin the inner planet all the way round once, then spin the outer one. Count how far each one travels.
Label each ring with how long that planet takes to go round once.
activities.title: The Desk-Top Solar System
activities.summary: Build the planets on wire arms so you can spin them and see who gets round the sun first.

learning.text: The outer planets have a much bigger loop to travel, and they also move more slowly along it. That is why one trip around the sun takes Earth a year, and takes Neptune about 165 of our years.
learning.title: Planets further from the sun take longer to go around it

activities.variation: Add a moon on a shorter arm that goes around one of your planets while the planet goes around the sun.
safetyNotes: A grown-up handles skewers or wire and blunts every sharp end with tape or a cork.

1. Using this site

You are welcome to use everything published here with the children in your care, at home, in a classroom, in a library, or in a community group.

By using the site you agree to these terms. If you are under eighteen, please read them with a grown-up.

2. Adult supervision and safety

Every activity states its own safety notes and says whether a child can lead it, needs a grown-up nearby, or needs a grown-up hands-on. Read those notes before you start.

You are responsible for judging whether an activity suits the child in front of you, the materials you have, and the space you are in. Making things involves scissors, glue, small parts, water, and occasionally a mess, and an adult has to decide what is appropriate.

We provide instructions. We do not supervise, and we are not responsible for injury, damage, or loss arising from doing an activity. Stop any activity that is not going well.

3. What you may do with our material

Printables, activity pages, and build cards may be printed and used freely for your own family, your own classroom, or a group session you are running.

  • Print as many copies as your family, class, or group needs
  • Adapt an activity and make your own version of it
  • Share a link to any page here with anyone

Please do not resell our files, republish them on another site as though they were yours, or strip the branding off them. A licence for a whole school or organisation is available; write to us.

4. What belongs to whom

The characters, illustrations, stories, episodes, written activities, and the design of this site belong to Chike's Creative Space.

What your child makes belongs to your child. We make no claim over anything created from one of our activities.

This is a prototype build. There is no checkout, no membership that can be joined, and no donation that can be taken. Prices shown are placeholders so the layout can be reviewed.

pages.body:
1. The short version

We do not ask children to sign up for anything. We do not build advertising profiles, and we do not sell anyone's information to anybody.

This build stores some information in a real, hosted database, not only inside your browser: an email address if you join the mailing list, the text of a message if you write to us, and the details listed below if a child sends in a story. Saved activities, recently viewed pages, and similar settings still live only in your own browser.

2. What this build stores, and where

Two different things happen depending on what you do on this site.

  • Activities you save with the heart button, activities and stories you have opened recently (capped at twelve), and which announcement banners you have closed live only in your own browser's storage. Clearing your browsing data erases these.

The forms below send what you type to a hosted database that we can read from an admin screen. That information does not disappear when you clear your browser.

  • Joining the mailing list stores the email address you give us.
  • Writing to us through the Grown-Ups contact form or the business contact form stores your message and the category you picked, and, for the business form, an organisation name if you gave one. Neither form currently asks for a reply-to email address.
  • Sending in a child's story stores a first name, the first letter of a last name, a town and state, a grown-up's email address (used once, to confirm a real person sent it), and the story text.
  • Content edits made in the prototype admin area are stored the same way.

3. The activity finder

The finder scores activities against the answers you give it using a fixed table of points, which is printed on the page underneath the results. The same answers always produce the same three suggestions.

Your answers are held in memory while you are on the page and are gone when you leave. They are not stored, not sent anywhere, and not used to build any kind of profile.

4. Where this data lives, and who could reach it

The database mentioned above is hosted by Supabase, a third-party database provider, rather than run on our own servers.

In this prototype build, that database is set up so it can be read and written using one shared access key that ships inside the site's own source code, the same way it does for any client-side app built this way. Right now, someone who obtained that key could read or change what is stored directly, bypassing this site and its own screens entirely.

We consider this an accepted, documented risk for a prototype with no real visitors yet, not something acceptable once the public can submit real information through these forms. It needs real accounts and stricter database rules before that happens.

5. Children

This site is written for children but designed to be arrived at by an adult.

The one place a child's own words reach us is the ‘Write a story’ form. We deliberately ask for as little as possible: a first name, the first letter of a last name (never a full name), a town and state (never a street address), and a grown-up's email address, used once, to confirm a real person sent it. No photograph or other upload is requested, and no full name is ever published.

A person reads every story before anything is published.

Beyond that one form, there is no child-facing account, no comment section, and no messaging between users.

A qualified legal review of whether this counts as collecting personal information from a child under laws such as the U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), and what that would require of us, has not happened yet. That review needs to happen before this goes live to the public.

6. Cookies and tracking

This build sets no cookies, loads no analytics, and includes no advertising or social tracking pixels.

It does load type from Google Fonts, which means a font request goes to Google's servers when you visit a page that uses one. The icon library is self-hosted already, and the fonts can be too if that matters to you.

7. Links to other sites

Some pages link out to YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, and Amazon. Once you follow one of those links you are on their site and their privacy policy applies, not ours. The shop links are ordinary search links, not affiliate links, in this build.

8. What is still to come

A live version will still need real accounts for members and a payment processor for anything sold. Neither exists yet: nothing on this site is an offer to sell, and there is no way to sign in as a member.

  • Which processor would handle payments, and what it would receive
  • How members' accounts would be protected
  • Stricter database rules, so a shared key can no longer read or write everything, as described above

None of that exists yet. When it does, this policy will be rewritten to describe it accurately, the same way this update replaced an earlier version that assumed nothing here left your browser.

9. Your rights

Depending on where you live, you may have the right to see, correct, export, or delete personal information a site holds about you.

For anything stored only in your own browser, clearing your browsing data does this yourself, immediately.

For a newsletter signup, a message you sent us, or a story submitted for a child, write to info@chikescreativespace.com and we will find, correct, or delete it by hand. There is no self-serve export or delete button for these yet; if that matters to you, please ask before using one of these forms.

body: A fact told to a child is a fact they can repeat. A fact discovered inside something they built is a fact they can use.

That is the whole reason our episodes start with a child making something rather than with a lesson. The paper airplane comes first. Altitude comes second, as the answer to a question the child is already asking.

Stories do the same work in a quieter way. A character who tries something, fails, and adjusts gives a child a rehearsal for their own frustration. It is much easier to try a fourth time when somebody in a book already tried a fourth time.
This is why every activity here ends with a question rather than a summary. The question is the part that carries.

body: Every episode we make is under two minutes and ends with something the viewer could go and build. That constraint is deliberate.
The measure we care about is not watch time. It is whether the screen goes off afterwards and something appears on the kitchen table.
If you want to help that along, do one thing: pause at the end and ask what they would make differently. Ten seconds of that turns a watched video into a plan.

body: Paper is the most forgiving material a child can start with. It is cheap, it is everywhere, and a mistake costs nothing more than another sheet.

A paper airplane teaches the most, because it gives an answer the moment you throw it. If it dives, something is wrong with the nose. If it turns, one wing is doing more work than the other. A child can read that feedback without anybody explaining it.
After that, try a pop-up card, a shadow puppet, a paper chain measured to the length of a room, and a folded box that actually holds something. Each one takes under half an hour.
The trick with all five is to resist demonstrating. Fold your own alongside theirs rather than fixing theirs. A wonky version they made themselves is worth more than a neat one you rescued.

characters.name: Chike

image.alt: Chike, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.tagline: Hmmm, what should we create today?
characters.storyValue: Chike is the curious, enthusiastic creative leader of the group. From his backyard treehouse, he codes games, builds inventions, draws ideas, and reads books that spark new questions. He quickly imagines what something could become and encourages friends to share their own ideas, though he is learning to slow down, listen, and test patiently. Every creation can become an adventure: a coded maze becomes a puzzle quest, a cardboard rover travels to space, or a weather book inspires a sky journey.
characters.relationship: Loves dreaming up new ideas in his treehouse Creative Lab.

characters.name: Zech

image.alt: Zech, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.tagline: One sheet of paper. A hundred possibilities.
characters.storyValue: Zech is Chike’s playful younger brother and Corey’s close friend. He loves transforming paper into airplanes, masks, maps, pop-up books, and imaginative inventions. He brings energy and bold ideas to every creation, but is learning that torn paper, mistakes, and restarts are all part of making. His paper projects open adventures in the sky, jungle, ocean, or anywhere his folds and drawings can lead.

characters.name: Mateo

image.alt: Mateo, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.outlet: Sculpting, building, and creating with recycled materials.
characters.tagline: If it can be stacked, it can be a city.
characters.strength: Sculpts and builds from almost any material
characters.storyValue: Mateo is Chike’s best friend and a thoughtful hands-on maker. He sees possibility in cardboard, clay, boxes, and everyday objects, turning them into volcanoes, creatures, cities, and sturdy structures. He is patient and resourceful, although he is learning to share unfinished work and welcome others’ ideas. His creations become adventures involving building, habitats, recycling, geology, and solving problems together.

characters.name: Kylah

image.alt: Kylah, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.tagline: Look closer. Then draw what you saw.
characters.storyValue: Kylah lives next door to Chike and notices details other kids often miss. With her sketchbook in hand, she draws animals, gardens, clouds, maps, and imaginative worlds inspired by the neighborhood. She is thoughtful and observant, but sometimes worries a picture is not ready to show. Through her adventures, Kylah learns that sharing a work in progress can be just as meaningful as revealing a finished masterpiece.

characters.name: Corey

image.alt: Corey, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.outlet: Toy play, world-building, and imaginative scenarios.
characters.tagline: Every toy is a character waiting for a story.
characters.storyValue: Corey is Zech’s friend, Stacey’s sibling, and one of Chike and Zech’s next-door neighbors. He turns toy cars, dinosaurs, blocks, and action figures into full stories, races, rescue missions, and exciting worlds. He is funny, energetic, and welcoming, though he is learning not to change the rules too quickly or take over a game. Corey’s toy adventures explore motion, fossils, maps, problem-solving, sharing, and taking turns.

characters.name: Stacey

image.alt: Stacey, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.tagline: If it makes a sound, it can make a song.
characters.storyValue: Stacey is Corey’s sibling and hears music everywhere—from rain on a window to footsteps on a sidewalk. She loves creating beats, singing songs, and listening closely to the sounds of nature. Calm and expressive, she is learning to trust her creative voice even when others do not immediately understand her idea. Her music leads to adventures about rhythm, vibrations, animal sounds, listening, and confidently expressing yourself.

characters.name: Averi

image.alt: Averi, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.tagline: Count the beat. Then let the beat carry you.
characters.strength: Is a dancer and an aspiring actress
characters.storyValue: Averi is an energetic performer who can turn a backyard, park, or school walkway into a stage. She enjoys ballet, line dancing, breakdancing, and acting out stories with movement. Bold and encouraging, Averi invites her friends into her imaginative performances, but she is learning that growth comes from practicing in public—not waiting for every move to be perfect. Her adventures explore rhythm, balance, movement, confidence, and celebrating different ways of expressing yourself.

characters.name: Yuna

image.alt: Yuna, drawn in the Creative Space comic style

characters.outlet: Reading, writing, character creation, and storytelling.
characters.tagline: Every good adventure starts on a page.
characters.storyValue: Yuna is a thoughtful reader and imaginative writer who always has a book, notebook, or story idea nearby. She creates characters, writes mysteries, develops riddles, and turns small neighborhood moments into big adventures. She listens carefully and sees connections others may overlook, but sometimes spends too long trying to plan the perfect ending. Yuna is learning that stories grow through starting, revising, and allowing new ideas to surprise her.
